papers.title: CFOs Meet LLMs
papers.abstract: Business sentiment is closely watched, but measurement is slow and costly: surveys reach a limited number of firms, arrive periodically, and take time to field and compile. We show that large language models hold the potential to address some of these shortcomings. We prompt an LLM to role-play as the CFO of a specific company on a specific date, for every public-company CFO who responded to the Duke–Federal Reserve CFO Survey from 2002- 2025. We find that LLM-generated forecasts reasonably match the cross-section of CFO expectations, with accuracy increasing with the amount of information provided to the LLM. We discuss the potential as well as the hurdles to using digital twins to mimic individual decision-makers.

papers.title: Beyond the First Best: Welfare and OPEC Market Power
papers.abstract: We introduce an empirical framework to quantify the welfare impact of market power, through coordinated production decisions by a cartel, while allowing for other distortions. We contrast two novel concepts – the marginal and the infra-marginal welfare loss – to a naive approach that fails to recognize the existence of other distortions operating alongside market power. We apply the framework to measure the impact of market power of OPEC in the global crude oil market. We leverage unique micro data on cost and production to quantify the deadweight loss and productive inefficiency due to the OPEC cartel. From 1970 onward, the naive approach implies that OPEC generated 2.2 trillion dollars of welfare losses, two-thirds from productive inefficiency and one-third from deadweight loss. Eliminating cost-minimization violations outside the cartel shrinks losses to around 0.7 trillion dollars, indicating that other frictions in the oil market are complementary to OPEC’s market power.

papers.title: Designing Low Emission Zones: Theory and Evidence
papers.abstract: Low Emission Zones (LEZs), which exclude polluting vehicles from parts of a city, are spreading. Yet how their design affects welfare is poorly understood. Unlike price instruments, LEZs ration access inefficiently, imposing costs on inframarginal drivers of restricted vehicles. In our model, welfare is quasi-convex in LEZ size, yielding bang-bang principles: LEZs should be as large as possible or not implemented at all; cleaner vehicles (e.g., hybrids) could be exempt as transition technologies but later restricted, which may require planner commitment. Using new-car purchases, we find Madrid’s LEZ shifted buyers toward cleaner cars, but the surplus losses of switchers and inframarginal drivers exceeded emission savings.

papers.title: Mental Models of Fiscal Policy
papers.abstract: We study how individuals form expectations about fiscal adjustment. Using survey data from more than 27,000 respondents across 13 countries, we jointly elicit beliefs about current fiscal conditions, expectations of tax increases and spending cuts, and open-ended explanations for those expectations. We classify these explanations into economic mental models, political narratives, and experience-based heuristics. Respondents reporting similar fiscal conditions nevertheless form systematically different expectations of adjustment. Economic mental models are associated with stronger expectations of tax increases and spending cuts in the fiscal configurations we examine, whereas experience-based reasoning is associated with weaker adjustment expectations. These differences are also reflected in intended economic behavior and portfolio allocations. In a randomized experiment, fiscal information increases the likelihood that respondents articulate economic reasoning, primarily among responses that would otherwise fall outside the three primary frameworks.

papers.title: How AI Impacts the Quest for Knowledge: Evidence from AlphaFold2
papers.abstract: Scientists can respond to artificial intelligence by pushing the frontier of science and asking new questions, or by deepening their understanding of questions already studied. We study how AI shapes this choice in structural biology, where experiments examine a protein's three-dimensional structure and its function. AlphaFold2, released in 2021, predicts the structure of almost every known protein, with a confidence that varies across proteins. Linking 530,471 proteins to the experiments run on them between 2017 and 2025, we compare how experimental activity changed after 2021 across proteins with more and less confident predictions. Where predictions are more confident, the experimental record adds fewer first structures for proteins far from any relative of known structure. It adds more follow-up experiments on proteins whose structure is already known, and the rise is largest for proteins surrounded by relatives of known structure. A model of experimental choice shows how AlphaFold2 can deepen existing knowledge rather than extend it: a prediction replaces an experiment that would establish a protein's structure, and it lowers the cost of experiments that build on that structure.

papers.title: Are Revealed Preferences All You Need for AI Alignment?
papers.abstract: AI agents learn what principals want from what principals choose. We offer a criterion for when a principal's decisions, at every belief an AI might hold, are all the AI needs. For acting, they are. Cautious actions, such as deferring to a person, typically divide the principal's actions into blocks, and for choosing costless evidence, decisions are enough exactly when the same evidence is best in every block. Otherwise, the AI acts as its principal would yet can gather the wrong evidence, and greater capability can turn that error into incorrect actions. Choices between two mistakes reveal what decisions miss.

papers.title: Bureaucratic Rigidity and Battle Outcomes: Evidence from Military Logistics in the Ming Dynasty
papers.abstract: Bureaucratic rules meant to improve accountability can undermine state effectiveness. We study a 1492 Ming dynasty reform that shifted military grain delivery from salt merchants to a state relay system with prefecture-to-prefecture handovers and fixed routes. Afterward, court records document more supply shortages at formerly merchant-supplied garrisons than at state-supplied ones. Using 406 defensive battles against foreign invaders, we find the reform reduced victory rates near these garrisons. Declines were largest where resupply mattered most (longer wars, walled-city defenses) and where the state’s rules were most costly (routes crossing more prefectures or exposed to floods, droughts, or rugged terrain).
